subject: Learning Methods
title: Teaching to an Imaginary Audience
description: A quick, practical guide to Teaching to an Imaginary Audience.

hook.text: Researchers found that students who explained material to a camera performed as well as those who taught a real person.

buildup.text: The audience doesn't need to be real. The act of formulating an external explanation activates the same deep processing.

discovery.text: Talking aloud forces you to linearize your knowledge. Thoughts in your head can be vague, but speech demands precision.

twist.text: Recording yourself adds accountability. You can replay it, catch errors, and hear where your explanation stumbles.

climax.text: Record a three-minute video explaining what you just studied. Watch it back. The stumbles are your study targets.

punchline.text: Record yourself teaching. Your stumbles are your guide.

quiz.question: Why does teaching to a camera work as well as teaching a real person?
options: Cameras create more social pressure than people
Formulating an external explanation activates the same deep processing
